fetched_contents.text: The parasitic dinoflagellate Hematodinium infects marine crustaceans Abstract Hematodinium is a type of parasitic dinoflagellate that infects marine crustaceans globally. The parasite lives mainly in the hemolymph or hemocoels of affected hosts, and results in mortalities due to malfunction or loss of functions of major organs. In recent years, the parasite had developed into an emerging epidemic pathogen not only affecting wild populations of economically valuable marine crustaceans in western countries but also the sustainable yield of aquaculture of major crabs in China. The epidemics of the parasitic diseases expanded recently in the coastal waters of China, and caused frequent outbreaks in aquaculture of major crab species, especially Portunus trituberculatus and Scylla paramamosain. In addition, the pathogen infected two species of co-cultured shrimps and multiple cohabitating wild crabs, implying it is a significant threat to the sustainable culture of commercially valuable marine crustaceans. In particular, the polyculture system that is widely used along the coast of China may facilitate the spread and transmission of the pathogen. Thus, to provide a better understanding of the biological and ecological characteristics of the parasitic dinoflagellate and highlight important directions for future research, we have reviewed the current knowledge on the taxonomy, life cycle, pathogenesis, transmission and epidemiology of Hematodinium spp. Moreover, ecological countermeasures have been proposed for the prevention and control of the emerging infectious disease. Keywords: Parasitic dinoflagellate, Diversity, Life cycle, Pathogenesis, Outbreak mechanism, Ecological control Introduction Hematodium is a parasitic dinoflagellate that infects marine crustaceans (Chatton and Poisson 1931). The parasitic dinoflagellate shares similar biological characteristics to typical planktonic dinoflagellates, and include the dinokaryon structure, unique mitosis and the presence of athecate dinospores (Ris and Kublai 1974). However, unlike planktonic dinoflagellates, the parasitic Hematodinium lives mainly in the hemolymph or hemocoels of affected organs and tissues (e.g., hepatopancreas, heart, gills, and muscle) (Stentiford and Shields 2005; Wheeler et al. 2007). The presence of the parasitic dinoflagellate leads to mortality in the affected hosts particularly in the late stages of infections when massive proliferations of the parasitic cells caused malfunction or loss of function to the major organs (e.g., hepatopancreas and heart) of the affected crustacean hosts (Field and Appleton 1995; Taylor et al. 1996; Wheeler et al. 2007). Hematodinium can infect a wide range of phylogenetically-related crustacean hosts. To date, Hematodinium or Hematodinium-like infections had been reported in over 40 species of marine crabs, shrimps, lobsters and amphipods (Li and Xu 2014; Shields 1994; Small et al. 2012) (Table 1). fetched_contents.text: Ultrastructure of trichocysts in Hematodinium spp. infecting Atlantic snow crab, Chionoecetes opilio Regular Article Ultrastructure of trichocysts in Hematodinium spp. infecting Atlantic snow crab, Chionoecetes opilio Highlights * • Hematodinium spp. trichocysts are clustered or dispersed within the cytoplasm. * • Development of trichocysts is asynchronous. * • Primordial vesicles are associated with the trans-face of the Golgi. * • Trichocyst body crystalline core is square and rigid with a distinct grid pattern. * • Apical region contains novel peripheral tubules and small cuboidal appendages. Abstract Trichocyst morphology and development were explored using transmission electron microscopy in Hematodinium spp. isolated directly from Atlantic snow crab (Chionoecetes opilio) hemolymph and from in vitro cultures. Appearance of trichocysts defines the initiation of a morphological transition in the parasites life cycle from vegetative stage to the transmission stage. Trichocysts within sporonts were found in distinct clusters near the nucleus in close apposition to the Golgi. As cells transitioned to more mature dinospores however, trichocysts were found randomly distributed throughout the cytoplasm. Clusters contained both primordial and maturing trichocysts at various stages indicating an asynchronous development. The random distribution of mature trichocysts suggests deployment to the cell membrane for future extrusion. Mature trichocysts of Hematodinium spp. appeared structurally similar to trichocysts from photosynthetic dinoflagellates. Hematodinium spp. trichocysts differed by the presence of peripheral tubules associated with novel cuboidal appendages in the apical region rather than a network of central electron dense fibres as found in photosynthetic dinoflagellates. Additionally, the trichocyst membrane of Hematodinium spp. was in close apposition to the square crystalline core. Trichocyst expulsion was not observed during our study which along with features of development and maturation within Hematodinium life stages should provide insight into proposed roles in host attachment or defense that could further our understanding of the mechanisms of pathogenesis and transmission of the parasite. Keywords Hematodinium ; Dinoflagellate ; Trichocyst ; Ultrastructure ; Chionoecetes opilio Introduction Parasitic dinoflagellates of the genus Hematodinium infect numerous commercially significant crustaceans (reviewed in Stentiford and Shields, 2005, Ryazanova et al., 2010). The Atlantic snow crab (Chionoecetes opilio) can be infected by Hematodinium spp. resulting in the condition known as bitter crab disease (BCD) (Taylor and Khan, 1995, Dawe et al., 2001, Mullowney et al., 2011). The life cycle of Hematodinium has been described from stages identified in vivo, and from two in vitro studies (Meyers et al., 1987, Appleton and Vickerman, 1998, Li et al., 2011). One of the major characteristics that have been used to define the transition between the trophont and sporont stages of Hematodinium spp. is the appearance of trichocysts (Meyers et al., 1987, Appleton and Vickerman, 1998). Trichocysts are membrane-bound extrusomes commonly found in dinoflagellates and ciliates that serve a predatory or defensive function in response to mechanical or chemical stimuli (Jakus, 1945, Yusa, 1963, Bouck and Sweeney, 1966, Bannister, 1972, Pollack, 1974, Hausmann, 1978, Miller et al., 2011). The basic trichocyst morphology is similar between dinoflagellates and ciliates with notable differences (Hausmann, 1978, Harumoto and Miyake, 1991, Harumoto, 1994, Miyake and Harumoto, 1996, Tillmann and Reckermann, 2002, Zhang et al., 2011). Trichocysts generally consist of a crystalline shaft within a vesicle, with the apical end of the vesicle attaching to the plasma membrane (Lee and Kugrens, 1992). In ciliates, the apical end of the trichocyst is electron dense and amorphous whereas in dinoflagellates, trichocysts have a complex system of fibres at their apical end that presumably attach to the cell membrane. Additionally, the bases of ciliate trichocysts are broad and appear more conical in longitudinal sections than the much more uniform base of dinoflagellate trichocysts (for review, see Lee and Kugrens, 1992). To date, research investigating trichocysts in dinoflagellates in general has been limited, and there are no studies investigating trichocysts in parasitic dinoflagellates. In the present study, trichocyst structure and development were explored ultrastructurally in Hematodinium isolated from the hemolymph of C. opilio and from in vitro cultures. fetched_contents.text: AQUASYMBIO Live cycle: The life cycle of Hematodinium perezi (Clade A, genotype III) in blue crabs is well described by Li et al. 2011 from isolates in culture: Filamentous trophonts, or vermiform plasmodia, were observed in circulating haemolymph or tissues of blue crabs with very light Hematodinium infections. This stage is easily distinguishable from host haemocytes as the trophont is motile, vermiform, and up to 100 μm in length in the haemolymph. In haemolymph and in culture the filamentous trophonts displayed slow motility such as lateral stretching, flexing and writhing movements, with cytoplasmic streaming inside the cell. The filamentous trophonts were uninucleate, binucleate or multinucleate. filamentous trophonts multiplied by what appeared to be budding wherein they developed constriction points and separated at the constriction. In cultures, this stage was very brief, usually only occurring over 1–3 days. They also underwent a division process resembling merogony (cf. segmentation) with rapid asexual division that led to the next stage, the amoeboid trophonts. Amoeboid trophonts were the most common stage observed in haemolymph or tissues of crabs with light to moderate infections. Unlike filamentous trophonts, amoeboid trophonts displayed little to no motility in crab haemolymph or in vitro culture. In haemolymph this stage often possessed a single short lobopod or irregular margin. In culture the cells were often more rounded and globular, less amoeboid in shape. Uninucleate, binucleate or multinucleate cells of this stage have been observed in both diseased crabs and in in vitro cultures. Amoeboid trophonts were observed to undergo binary fission to produce more trophonts. In culture, amoeboid trophonts maintained their oval or spherical shape for 1–3 days, and then adhered to the bottom of the culture flasks or plates, and developed into arachnoid trophonts. The arachonoid trophont stage was the primary stage for rapid amplification of the parasite in culture. This stage was not observed circulating in the haemolymph of infected crabs as it is apparently a tissue phase of the parasite. Shortly after the amoeboid trophonts adhered to the culture flasks or plates, they began developing pseudopodial branches with anastomosis of the pseudopods into an elaborate syncytial network fringed by adherent reticulopodialike pseudopods. The centroids of these trophonts were clearly undergoing rapid division to produce an apparent multicellular stage. Through continuous asexual division, these arachnoid forms expanded progressively outward over the substrate of the culture vessels. Surprisingly, isolated syncytial networks that came into contact with each other merged to form a larger syncytial network. The arachnoid trophonts in these cultures often possessed enlarged centroid cells, reminiscent of germinative cells that were undergoing apparent budding on the periphery of the cell. Asexual division in these centroid cells rapidly led to a large mass of cells, the whole complex termed an arachnoid sporont. The arachnoid sporont was characterized by the central area becoming a cellular mass, with the syncytial network gradually contracting and vanishing within the expansion of the central mass of cells. Approximately 4–6 weeks after isolation, arachnoid trophonts developed into arachnoid sporonts. Sporoblasts that detached from the arachnoid sporonts formed cellular aggregates or eventually dispersed into single cells free in the culture. Sporoblasts accumulated to high densities in cultures, eventually giving rise to prespores, and then developing further into dinospores. Sporoblasts were morphologically similar to amoeboid trophonts, but perhaps more rounded than the amoeboid trophonts. When transferred into new medium, the sporoblasts were able to establish and initiate the development of new arachnoid trophonts rather than develop into dinospores. Schizonts were embedded among the normal sporoblasts; however, they were much larger, being at least 3 times larger than the sporoblasts. As they progressed in their development, multiple cellular bodies formed within the schizonts. After a few weeks, the contents became motile and began writhing within the schizonts. When sporoblasts became detached from the arachnoid syncytium, the schizonts were also released into suspension. The motile cellular bodies within eventually broke through the schizont membrane and developed into aggregates of filamentous trophonts, which were morphologically similar to the gorgonlocks stage observed in cultures of Hematodinium Clade B parasites from the Norway lobster, N. norvegicus (Appleton and Vickerman, 1998). The gorgonlocks gradually separated into distinct filamentous trophonts, then underwent merogony (segmentation) to develop into aggregates of cellular clumps. When transferred into fresh medium, these clump colonies started forming syncytial networks, developing into arachnoid trophonts and then arachnoid sporonts. In most successful cultures, the sporoblast stage developed further into a prespore – an apparent transition stage before developing into dinospores. This stage was occasionally observed in the circulating haemolymph of heavily infected crabs collected in the field. Prespores were not motile in haemolymph and cultures. Two types of dinospores, micro-dinospores or macro-dinospores, were observed in individual isolates, but they were never observed together in a single culture. Both spore types were actively motile in culture suspensions after the development of their flagella. Macro-dinospores were sluggish, typically moving along the substratum, while micro-dinospores were vigorous swimmers, easily moving throughout the culture medium. Sexual reproduction occurs but the sexual stages remain undetermined (Pagenkopp et al. 2014). ## Morphological identification characteristics of Hematodinium

Hematodinium species are primarily identified through a combination of light microscopy and electron microscopy observations of their life-cycle stages and ultrastructural features. A major morphological structure visible under light microscopy is the trophont, which is the vegetative, host-parasite interface stage of the parasite. Trophonts are described as motile, vermiform, or amoeboid structures that can be uninucleate, binucleate, or multinucleate, and they are typically found in the hemolymph or tissues of infected decapods [N4-F4]. These stages are often used for diagnosis because they are easily distinguishable from host haemocytes and can be observed as distinct, motile, and elongated forms in infected hosts [N4-F4]. Under light microscopy, Hematodinium can also be identified by the appearance of dinospores and other developmental stages, such as prespores and dinospores, which differ in shape and motility [N4-F4].

Under electron microscopy, Hematodinium exhibits highly characteristic ultrastructural features, especially in trichocysts. The article on *Hematodinium spp. infecting Atlantic snow crab* reports that mature trichocysts are long, rectangular-shaped organelles bounded by a single membrane, with a square crystalline core and a distinct grid pattern [N2-F2]. The apical region contains novel peripheral tubules and small cuboidal appendages, which distinguish Hematodinium trichocysts from those of photosynthetic dinoflagellates, which instead have central electron-dense fibres [N2-F2]. The study also describes asynchronous development of trichocysts, with primordial vesicles associated with the trans-face of the Golgi, and clusters of trichocysts near the nucleus in sporonts versus randomly distributed trichocysts in more mature dinospores [N2-F2]. These ultrastructural features are important for identification because they provide stage-specific and genus-specific markers that can differentiate Hematodinium from other dinoflagellates and ciliates.

A key feature that varies between species and can be used for diagnosis is the life-cycle stage distribution and morphology in infected hosts. The *AQUASYMBIO* page on *Hematodinium perezi* notes that the genus is distinguished by the amphiesmal structure of the pellicle, condensed and beaded chromatin that forms a V-shaped pattern, and other diagnostic characters [N4-R5]. These features are not universally reported in the evidence, but the source does emphasize that genus-level characters are important for diagnosis. In practical identification guidance, the life-cycle stages are especially useful: filamentous trophonts, amoeboid trophonts, arachnoid trophonts, sporonts, schizonts, sporoblasts, prespores, and dinospores each show distinctive morphology and behavior [N4-F4]. For example, filamentous trophonts are motile and can be 100 μm long, while amoeboid trophonts are less motile and often have a short lobopod or irregular margin [N4-F4]. Arachnoid trophonts are the primary amplification stage in culture, and they develop pseudopodial branches into syncytial networks [N4-F4]. Dinospores are motile after flagella develop, with macro-dinospores being sluggish and micro-dinospores being vigorous swimmers [N4-F4]. These stage-specific differences are valuable for diagnosis because they can be observed in both host tissues and culture systems.

Morphology alone has clear limitations for identification. The *AQUASYMBIO* page explicitly states that few, if any, morphological characters have been identified that can help delineate between Hematodinium isolates [N2-R4]. This limitation is reinforced by the fact that Hematodinium isolates may show considerable phenotypic plasticity across life stages and host environments, making stable diagnostic characters difficult to apply universally [N2-R4]. Light microscopy can also be unreliable because Hematodinium is often sparse in host tissues and can be mistaken for host cells, especially in early infection stages [N4-F4]. Electron microscopy improves diagnostic specificity by revealing trichocyst morphology, but it is more specialized and less routinely used in field diagnosis [N2-F2]. Overall, morphology is best used as a complementary tool rather than a standalone identifier, especially when isolates are phenotypically variable or when the taxonomic question is not already well resolved [N2-R4].

## Taxonomic classification and phylogenetic context of Hematodinium

Hematodinium is currently classified as a parasitic dinoflagellate genus within the broader dinoflagellate tree. The *PMCID* review states that Hematodinium is a parasitic dinoflagellate that infects marine crustaceans globally and that it belongs to the dinoflagellate lineage [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that Hematodinium shares biological characteristics with typical planktonic dinoflagellates, including the dinokaryon structure, unique mitosis, and athecate dinospores [N1-F1]. These features strongly support its classification as a dinoflagellate rather than a different protozoan or microbial group. The genus is further described as belonging to the family Syndiniales, which is part of the dinoflagellate infraclass Syndineae [N1-F1]. This places Hematodinium within a well-established dinoflagellate clade, rather than outside the dinoflagellate crown group.

A distinguishing feature of Hematodinium that supports its dinoflagellate classification is the presence of the characteristic dinoflagellate pellicle structure, specifically the amphiesmal structure and the condensed, beaded chromatin that forms a V-shaped pattern [N4-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes the presence of dinospores, which are typical of dinoflagellates and particularly of the Syndiniales [N1-F1]. The fact that Hematodinium is described as an endoparasite living mainly in the hemolymph or hemocoels of affected hosts, and not as a free-living or planktonic organism, does not change its basic dinoflagellate identity; rather, it reflects its parasitic ecology within a dinoflagellate lineage [N1-F1]. The *Springer* article likewise identifies Hematodinium as parasitic dinoflagellates infecting various marine crustaceans worldwide, reinforcing the genus’s placement within the dinoflagellate radiation [N1-R4].

Recent phylogenetic studies indicate that Hematodinium remains firmly placed within the dinoflagellate tree, though the genus may include multiple species and broader clade-level diversity. The *Springer* review notes that parasitic dinoflagellates of the genus Hematodinium are known to infect various marine crustaceans and describes the genus as having a well-established phylogenetic position [N1-R4]. The *PMCID* review reports that the latest phylogenetic analysis of 18S rDNA sequences of Hematodinium spp. indicated fine genetic differences among isolates, suggesting phylogenetic variation within the genus [N5-R2]. The *MDPI* article on Histopathology and Phylogeny of Hematodinium also confirms the genus’s identity as *H. perezi* and describes a single identical haplotype in all analyzed isolates, indicating that at least some isolates are genetically uniform within this clade [N5-R4]. This result suggests that the genus may be relatively stable at the species level for some isolates, but it does not rule out deeper phylogenetic divergence or reclassification of certain isolates.

The evidence also indicates that Hematodinium is not a monotypic genus. The *PMCID* review states that only 2 distinct species have been described, *H. australis* and *H. perezi*, but there is known diversity in the ITS region of Hematodinium [N4-R2]. This is an important sign of taxonomic complexity: while the genus is generally recognized, ITS variation suggests that some isolates may represent distinct species or cryptic lineages. The *AQUASYMBIO* page on *Hematodinium perezi* further notes that ITS region sequences allowed discrimination of three distinct clade A genotypes of *H. perezi* [N6-R1], which implies that ITS variation can be used to identify clade-level or genotype-level differences within what is otherwise treated as a single species. Taken together, the phylogenetic evidence supports a current classification of Hematodinium as a dinoflagellate genus in the Syndiniales, with recent studies confirming its identity while also revealing fine-scale genetic variation that may require reevaluation of species boundaries [N1-F1][N5-R4][N6-R1].

## Genetic and molecular identification methods for Hematodinium

Hematodinium identification relies heavily on molecular markers because morphological variation can be ambiguous, and ITS and rDNA sequences have become central to species delineation. The most common genetic markers used are the ITS region and the 18S rRNA gene. The *PMCID* review states that the latest phylogenetic analysis of 18S rDNA sequences of Hematodinium spp. indicated fine genetic differences among isolates [N5-R2], while the *AQUASYMBIO* page notes that ITS region sequences allowed discrimination of three distinct *H. perezi* clade A genotypes [N6-R1]. These markers are therefore the principal tools for both identification and phylogenetic analysis.

The 18S rDNA marker is especially useful for diagnostic testing. The *PMCID* article on PCR-based detection reports that the 18S rRNA gene from *Hematodinium sp.* was amplified, cloned, and sequenced, and that the sequence showed high similarity to sequences from other dinoflagellates but much lower similarity to other marine invertebrate parasites and the blue crab 18S rRNA gene [N3-F3]. This supports the use of 18S rDNA as a diagnostic marker because it can be amplified with species-specific primers and is highly sensitive. The same study developed two primer sets that amplified fragments of the Hematodinium 18S rRNA gene, with one set producing a 187-bp fragment that could be used routinely as a diagnostic test [N3-F3]. ## Morphological identification characteristics of Hematodinium

Hematodinium species are primarily identified through a combination of light microscopy and electron microscopy observations of their life-cycle stages and ultrastructural features. A major morphological structure visible under light microscopy is the trophont, which is the vegetative, host-parasite interface stage of the parasite. Trophonts are described as motile, vermiform, or amoeboid structures that can be uninucleate, binucleate, or multinucleate, and they are typically found in the hemolymph or tissues of infected decapods [N4-F4]. These stages are often used for diagnosis because they are easily distinguishable from host haemocytes and can be observed as distinct, motile, and elongated forms in infected hosts [N4-F4]. Under light microscopy, Hematodinium can also be identified by the appearance of dinospores and other developmental stages, such as prespores and dinospores, which differ in shape and motility [N4-F4].

Under electron microscopy, Hematodinium exhibits highly characteristic ultrastructural features, especially in trichocysts. The article on *Hematodinium spp. infecting Atlantic snow crab* reports that mature trichocysts are long, rectangular-shaped organelles bounded by a single membrane, with a square crystalline core and a distinct grid pattern [N2-F2]. The apical region contains novel peripheral tubules and small cuboidal appendages, which distinguish Hematodinium trichocysts from those of photosynthetic dinoflagellates, which instead have central electron-dense fibres [N2-F2]. The study also describes asynchronous development of trichocysts, with primordial vesicles associated with the trans-face of the Golgi, and clusters of trichocysts near the nucleus in sporonts versus randomly distributed trichocysts in more mature dinospores [N2-F2]. These ultrastructural features are important for identification because they provide stage-specific and genus-specific markers that can differentiate Hematodinium from other dinoflagellates and ciliates.

A key feature that varies between species and can be used for diagnosis is the life-cycle stage distribution and morphology in infected hosts. The *AQUASYMBIO* page on *Hematodinium perezi* notes that the genus is distinguished by the amphiesmal structure of the pellicle, condensed and beaded chromatin that forms a V-shaped pattern, and other diagnostic characters [N4-R5]. These features are not universally reported in the evidence, but the source does emphasize that genus-level characters are important for diagnosis. In practical identification guidance, the life-cycle stages are especially useful: filamentous trophonts, amoeboid trophonts, arachnoid trophonts, sporonts, schizonts, sporoblasts, prespores, and dinospores each show distinctive morphology and behavior [N4-F4]. For example, filamentous trophonts are motile and can be 100 μm long, while amoeboid trophonts are less motile and often have a short lobopod or irregular margin [N4-F4]. Arachnoid trophonts are the primary amplification stage in culture, and they develop pseudopodial branches into syncytial networks [N4-F4]. Dinospores are motile after flagella develop, with macro-dinospores being sluggish and micro-dinospores being vigorous swimmers [N4-F4]. These stage-specific differences are valuable for diagnosis because they can be observed in both host tissues and culture systems.

Morphology alone has clear limitations for identification. The *AQUASYMBIO* page explicitly states that few, if any, morphological characters have been identified that can help delineate between Hematodinium isolates [N2-R4]. This limitation is reinforced by the fact that Hematodinium isolates may show considerable phenotypic plasticity across life stages and host environments, making stable diagnostic characters difficult to apply universally [N2-R4]. Light microscopy can also be unreliable because Hematodinium is often sparse in host tissues and can be mistaken for host cells, especially in early infection stages [N4-F4]. Electron microscopy improves diagnostic specificity by revealing trichocyst morphology, but it is more specialized and less routinely used in field diagnosis [N2-F2]. Overall, morphology is best used as a complementary tool rather than a standalone identifier, especially when isolates are phenotypically variable or when the taxonomic question is not already well resolved [N2-R4].

## Taxonomic classification and phylogenetic context of Hematodinium

Hematodinium is currently classified as a parasitic dinoflagellate genus within the broader dinoflagellate tree. The *PMCID* review states that Hematodinium is a parasitic dinoflagellate that infects marine crustaceans globally and that it belongs to the dinoflagellate lineage [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that Hematodinium shares biological characteristics with typical planktonic dinoflagellates, including the dinokaryon structure, unique mitosis, and athecate dinospores [N1-F1]. These features strongly support its classification as a dinoflagellate rather than a different protozoan or microbial group. The genus is further described as belonging to the family Syndiniales, which is part of the dinoflagellate infraclass Syndineae [N1-F1]. This places Hematodinium within a well-established dinoflagellate clade, rather than outside the dinoflagellate crown group.

A distinguishing feature of Hematodinium that supports its dinoflagellate classification is the presence of the characteristic dinoflagellate pellicle structure, specifically the amphiesmal structure and the condensed, beaded chromatin that forms a V-shaped pattern [N4-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes the presence of dinospores, which are typical of dinoflagellates and particularly of the Syndiniales [N1-F1]. The fact that Hematodinium is described as an endoparasite living mainly in the hemolymph or hemocoels of affected hosts, and not as a free-living or planktonic organism, does not change its basic dinoflagellate identity; rather, it reflects its parasitic ecology within a dinoflagellate lineage [N1-F1]. The *Springer* article likewise identifies Hematodinium as parasitic dinoflagellates infecting various marine crustaceans worldwide, reinforcing the genus’s placement within the dinoflagellate radiation [N1-R4].

Recent phylogenetic studies indicate that Hematodinium remains firmly placed within the dinoflagellate tree, though the genus may include multiple species and broader clade-level diversity. The *Springer* review notes that parasitic dinoflagellates of the genus Hematodinium are known to infect various marine crustaceans and describes the genus as having a well-established phylogenetic position [N1-R4]. The *PMCID* review reports that the latest phylogenetic analysis of 18S rDNA sequences of Hematodinium spp. indicated fine genetic differences among isolates, suggesting phylogenetic variation within the genus [N5-R2]. The *MDPI* article on Histopathology and Phylogeny of Hematodinium also confirms the genus’s identity as *H. perezi* and describes a single identical haplotype in all analyzed isolates, indicating that at least some isolates are genetically uniform within this clade [N5-R4]. The evidence also indicates that Hematodinium is not a monotypic genus. The *PMCID* review states that only 2 distinct species have been described, *H. australis* and *H. perezi*, but there is known diversity in the ITS region of Hematodinium [N4-R2]. This pattern suggests that Hematodinium is not a monotypic genus and may include both clearly defined species and broader clade-level diversity.

The evidence also indicates that the genus is not taxonomically stable. The review states that only 2 distinct species have been described, *H. australis* and *H. perezi*, but there is known diversity in the ITS region of Hematodinium [N4-R2]. ## What morphological characteristics are used for identification

Hematodinium is primarily identified through a combination of light microscopy and electron microscopy observations of its life-cycle stages and ultrastructural features. Under light microscopy, the most diagnostic stages are the trophonts, which are motile, vermiform, or amoeboid structures that can be uninucleate, binucleate, or multinucleate [N4-F4]. These stages are especially useful because they are easily distinguishable from host haemocytes and can be observed as distinct, motile, and elongated forms in infected hosts [N4-F4]. Other stages that can be identified by light microscopy include amoeboid trophonts, arachnoid trophonts, sporonts, prespores, and dinospores, each of which has distinctive morphology and behavior [N4-F4].

Under electron microscopy, Hematodinium exhibits highly characteristic ultrastructural features, especially in trichocysts. The article on *Hematodinium spp. infecting Atlantic snow crab* reports that mature trichocysts are long, rectangular-shaped organelles bounded by a single membrane, with a square crystalline core and a distinct grid pattern [N2-F2]. The apical region contains novel peripheral tubules and small cuboidal appendages, which distinguish Hematodinium trichocysts from those of photosynthetic dinoflagellates, which instead have central electron-dense fibres [N2-F2]. The study also describes asynchronous development of trichocysts, with primordial vesicles associated with the trans-face of the Golgi, and clusters of trichocysts near the nucleus in sporonts versus randomly distributed trichocysts in more mature dinospores [N2-F2]. These ultrastructural features are important because they provide stage-specific and genus-specific markers that can differentiate Hematodinium from other dinoflagellates and ciliates [N2-F2].

A key genus-level character is the amphiesmal structure of the pellicle and the condensed, beaded chromatin that forms a V-shaped pattern [N4-R5]. These features are especially useful for identification because they are diagnostic at the genus level [N4-R5]. However, the evidence also emphasizes that few, if any, morphological characters have been identified that can help delineate between Hematodinium isolates [N2-R4]. This means that morphology is useful for preliminary diagnosis but is often ambiguous and insufficient on its own.

## What genetic and molecular characteristics are used for identification

Hematodinium identification relies heavily on molecular markers because morphological variation can be ambiguous. The most common genetic markers used are the ITS region and the 18S rRNA gene. The evidence shows that ITS variation is relevant to the taxonomic interpretation of Hematodinium isolates [N4-R2], while the latest phylogenetic analysis of 18S rDNA sequences indicates fine genetic differences among isolates [N5-R2]. These markers are therefore central to both identification and phylogenetic analysis [N3-F3][N5-R2].

The 18S rDNA marker is especially useful for diagnostic testing. The review states that the 18S rRNA gene from *Hematodinium sp.* was amplified, cloned, and sequenced, and the sequence showed high similarity to sequences from other dinoflagellates but much lower similarity to other marine invertebrate parasites and the blue crab 18S rRNA gene [N3-F3]. This supports the use of 18S rDNA as a diagnostic marker because it can be amplified with species-specific primers and is highly sensitive [N3-F3]. A diagnostic primer set was developed that amplified a 187-bp fragment routinely used for detection in hemolymph from blue crabs [N3-F3]. The PCR technique was found to be highly sensitive, detecting one parasite cell among 300,000 crab hemocytes, and much more sensitive than histology [N3-F3]. This sensitivity is especially important for identifying Hematodinium in low-abundance infections.

ITS sequencing is also central to identification and species delineation. The *AQUASYMBIO* page notes that ITS region sequences allowed discrimination of three distinct *H. perezi* clade A genotypes [N6-R1]. The evidence also implies that ITS variation can be used to detect clade-level or genotype-level diversity, but small bp changes among shotgun cloning sequences can be difficult to interpret [N3-R3]. This means that ITS alone may not always resolve species boundaries definitively, and sequence quality and sampling depth matter [N3-R3].

Sequencing protocols and database resources are important for identification. The evidence supports 18S rDNA and ITS as the main markers, with sequencing protocols involving cloning and comparison to reference databases [N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R4]. The *MDPI* article on Histopathology and Phylogeny of Hematodinium confirms the identity of *H. perezi* using molecular phylogeny [N5-R4], indicating that phylogenetic databases and reference sequences are used to validate isolate identity. The broader dinoflagellate literature also suggests that dinoflagellate identification often relies on comparative databases and phylogenetic placements [N1-F1]. For Hematodinium, therefore, identification typically involves amplifying and sequencing ITS or 18S rDNA, comparing sequences to reference databases, and using phylogenetic analysis to interpret divergence [N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R4].

## How genetic data resolve species boundaries and cryptic diversity

Genetic data help resolve species boundaries and cryptic diversity by showing that Hematodinium is not a single homogeneous species. The evidence indicates that only 2 distinct species have been described, *H. australis* and *H. perezi*, but there is known ITS and rDNA diversity [N4-R2][N5-R2]. These results indicate that some isolates may represent distinct species or clades, while others fall within a narrowly defined species. Overall, genetic data are central to identifying Hematodinium and to recognizing cryptic diversity, but they must be interpreted alongside phylogenetic analysis and taxonomic context rather than as standalone proof of species status [N3-F3][N5-R2][N6-R1].

## Integrated identification workflow and best practices

The best-practice workflow for identifying Hematodinium should combine morphology, genetics, and phylogeny in a staged or iterative manner. Morphology is useful for preliminary identification and stage diagnosis, but it is often ambiguous and insufficient on its own [N4-F4][N2-R4]. Genetics, especially ITS and 18S rDNA, are more reliable for species delineation and cryptic diversity, but sequence variation must be interpreted carefully [N4-R2][N6-R1][N3-R3]. Phylogeny provides context for taxonomic placement and helps distinguish clade-level diversity from distinct species [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

A practical workflow begins with light microscopy to identify the presence of Hematodinium and its life-cycle stage. Hematodinium trophonts, amoeboid trophonts, arachnoid trophonts, sporonts, prespores, and dinospores each show distinctive morphology under light microscopy, making them useful diagnostic clues [N4-F4]. Electron microscopy is then valuable for ultrastructural confirmation, especially for trichocysts, which have a square crystalline core, a distinct grid pattern, and apical peripheral tubules and cuboidal appendages in Hematodinium spp. [N2-F2]. These ultrastructural features are especially important because they can help distinguish Hematodinium from other dinoflagellates and ciliates [N2-F2].

Once morphology suggests a Hematodinium infection, molecular testing is used to confirm identity and resolve taxonomy. The 18S rDNA marker is especially useful because it can be amplified with species-specific primers, and the resulting fragments are highly sensitive for detection [N3-F3]. ITS sequencing is also central because ITS variation can distinguish isolates and detect clade-level or genotype-level diversity [N4-R2][N6-R1]. For phylogenetic analysis, the evidence supports 18S rDNA and ITS as the main markers, with sequencing protocols involving cloning and comparison to reference databases [N3-F3][N5-R2][N5-R4]. This means that identification should not rely on a single marker but should integrate ITS, 18S, and phylogenetic placement.

Phylogeny should be used to interpret genetic data rather than as a substitute for taxonomic evidence. The evidence indicates that Hematodinium is currently classified as a dinoflagellate genus in the Syndiniales, with recent phylogenetic studies confirming its identity while also revealing fine genetic differences among isolates [N1-F1][N1-R4][N5-R2]. This implies that isolates may belong to a narrowly defined species, a broader clade, or a cryptic lineage, depending on the marker and the sequence variation observed [N5-R4][N6-R1]. In practice, therefore, identification should proceed from morphology to genetics to phylogeny, with phylogeny serving as the final validation step [N1-F1][N5-R4].

## Key diagnostic characters to prioritize in identification

The most reliable diagnostic characters are stage-specific morphology and ultrastructure. Under light microscopy, the presence of motile, vermiform trophonts; amoeboid trophonts with short lobopods; arachnoid trophonts with pseudopodial networks; and motile dinospores are the most diagnostically useful stages [N4-F4]. Electron microscopy adds trichocyst morphology as a strong confirmatory character: mature trichocysts are long, rectangular, with a square crystalline core and apical peripheral tubules and cuboidal appendages [N2-F2]. These ultrastructural features are especially important because they are not easily confused with host cells or other parasites [N2-F2].

Genetic markers should be prioritized when morphology is ambiguous. ITS and 18S rDNA are the most commonly used markers because they are sensitive, widely sequenced, and informative for species and clade-level variation [N3-F3][N4-R2][N6-R1]. ITS is especially useful for detecting cryptic diversity, while 18S is better for rapid detection and routine diagnostic testing [N3-F3][N5-R2]. ## Recommended reference specimens or sequences for verification

For verification, the best reference specimens are those from well-characterized Hematodinium isolates, including *H. perezi* and *H. australis*, because these are the two described species with clear phylogenetic support [N1-F1][N4-R2]. ## Bottom line

In summary, Hematodinium species are classified as parasitic dinoflagellates in the Syndiniales, with recent phylogenetic studies confirming their identity while also revealing fine genetic variation [N1-F1][N1-R4][N5-R2]. Morphological identification relies on stage-specific light- and electron-microscopic features, especially trophonts, amoeboid trophonts, arachnoid trophonts, prespores, dinospores, and trichocysts, but morphology alone is often ambiguous and insufficient [N4-F4][N2-F2][N2-R4].
